analysis.investment_thesis: Maharashtra Scooters is a financial holding company — explicitly excluded from the Magic Formula — with Earnings Yield of ~0.9% (EBIT ₹170 Cr / EV ~₹18,730 Cr) and ROIC of ~0.5%, both catastrophically below the 12% and 20% thresholds respectively. The sole interesting data point is a 55% discount to book (P/B 0.45x), but that metric belongs to Graham's framework, not Greenblatt's.
key_strengths: P/B of 0.45x implies ~55% discount to NAV (₹34,588 Cr assets vs ₹15,007 Cr market cap) — a classic holdco discount.
Near-zero capex business with 4/4 years of positive OCF (₹159–209 Cr range); FCF converts 1:1 to net profit.
51% promoter holding (Bajaj group) provides governance stability; growing net profit CAGR of 14.5%.
key_risks: Magic Formula explicitly excludes financial/investment holding companies — both ROIC (0.55%) and Earnings Yield (~0.9%) are meaningless for capital allocation here.
Revenue declined -1.9% CAGR (2022–2025) to ₹183 Cr; EBITDA collapsed -9.6% CAGR — underlying investment income is shrinking.
P/S of 47.87x and EV/EBITDA of 47.84x confirm the stock is priced as a pure NAV play, not an earnings compounder — holdco discounts can persist indefinitely.
red_flags: Financial holding company — Magic Formula does not apply; ROIC and Earnings Yield are structurally near-zero.
ROE of 0.69% on ₹30,863 Cr equity: capital is almost entirely idle investment securities generating negligible operating returns.
EBITDA fell sharply to ₹128 Cr in FY25 from ₹204 Cr in FY24 — a 37% single-year drop not explained by revenue alone.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From a Magic Formula standpoint, Maharashtra Scooters is an automatic disqualification. Greenblatt's framework was built to rank operating businesses on Earnings Yield (EBIT/EV) and Return on Capital (EBIT / NWC + Net Fixed Assets). Here, EBIT of ₹170 Cr against an enterprise value of roughly ₹18,730 Cr yields an Earnings Yield of ~0.9% — versus my 12% minimum threshold. ROIC is equally meaningless: the ₹34,588 Cr balance sheet is almost entirely investment securities, not productive operating capital, giving ROCE of just 0.55%. This is why Greenblatt explicitly removes financial companies from the screen.

The only analytically interesting feature is the 55% discount to book value (P/B 0.45x), which is a classic Bajaj group holdco structure where listed subsidiaries hold equity stakes far exceeding their market cap. But that thesis belongs to Ben Graham or event-driven arbitrage — not the Magic Formula. Net profit growing 14.5% CAGR to ₹214 Cr is entirely driven by mark-to-market or dividend income on the investment portfolio, not by any improvement in the underlying business franchise. I have no edge here, and the framework simply does not apply.
